headings.title: Introduction to Coronary Circulation
headings.content: The heart is a hardworking muscular pump that beats continuously throughout a person's life. Despite pumping blood through all chambers of the body, the heart muscle cannot extract oxygen and nutrients directly from the blood it pumps. Instead, it relies on its own dedicated network of blood vessels known as the **coronary circulation**. This vascular system ensures the myocardium receives a constant, rich supply of oxygenated blood to meet its high metabolic demands. Without this specialized blood supply, cardiac muscle cells quickly suffer from lack of oxygen and begin to lose their ability to contract effectively.

headings.title: Anatomy of the Coronary Arteries and Veins
headings.content: The **coronary arteries** branch directly from the base of the ascending aorta, just above the aortic valve. The **left main coronary artery** divides into the **left anterior descending artery** (LAD), which supplies the anterior wall and septum, and the **left circumflex artery**, which feeds the lateral wall. The **right coronary artery** (RCA) primarily supplies the right ventricle and the inferior wall of the heart. On the venous side, deoxygenated blood is collected by cardiac veins that run parallel to the arteries. These veins merge to form the **coronary sinus**, which empties directly into the right atrium.

headings.title: Myocardial Blood Supply and Perfusion Mechanics
headings.content: Unlike most other tissues in the body that receive blood during systole, the left ventricle receives the majority of its blood flow during **diastole**. When the heart muscle contracts during systole, the intense mechanical squeezing compresses the small intramyocardial blood vessels, temporarily halting flow. Once the heart relaxes in diastole, this compression is released, allowing blood to surge into the coronary capillary beds. Therefore, a very low diastolic blood pressure or a dangerously fast heart rate can drastically reduce the time available for coronary filling and myocardial perfusion.

headings.title: Physiological Regulation of Coronary Blood Flow
headings.content: Coronary blood flow is tightly controlled to match the changing metabolic needs of the heart. The primary regulatory mechanism is **local metabolic control**. When the myocardium works harder, it consumes more oxygen and releases vasodilator metabolites such as adenosine, hydrogen ions, and carbon dioxide into the interstitial fluid. These substances relax the smooth muscle in the walls of the coronary arterioles, causing them to widen and increase blood flow. Conversely, the autonomic nervous system provides neural fine-tuning, though local chemical signals override nervous control during heavy exertion.

headings.title: Coronary Artery Disease and Ischemia
headings.content: When coronary arteries become narrowed or blocked by **atherosclerosis**, blood flow cannot keep up with myocardial demand. This mismatch leads to **myocardial ischemia**, where heart cells are starved of adequate oxygen and nutrients. Ischemia causes chest pain known as **angina pectoris** and disrupts normal electrical and mechanical heart function. If a coronary vessel becomes completely occluded by a blood clot, the affected heart muscle tissue dies, resulting in a **myocardial infarction** or heart attack.

headings.title: Assessment and Diagnostic Evaluation in Nursing
headings.content: Nurses play a vital role in detecting compromised coronary circulation by performing focused cardiovascular assessments. They evaluate chest pain characteristics using the standard OPQRST mnemonic and monitor vital signs for hemodynamic instability. Diagnostic tools include a 12-lead **electrocardiogram** (ECG) to identify ST-segment changes indicative of ischemia or injury. Blood tests measuring **cardiac biomarkers** such as troponin are essential to confirm whether myocardial cell damage has occurred. Nurses also prepare patients for definitive imaging procedures like coronary angiography.

headings.title: Nursing Management and Patient Care Interventions
headings.content: Care for patients with impaired coronary circulation focuses on restoring the balance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand. Nurses administer prescribed medications such as **nitroglycerin** to promote vasodilation and relieve chest pain, along with supplemental oxygen if oxygen saturation is low. Continuous cardiac monitoring helps detect lethal arrhythmias early. Long-term management involves educating the patient on lifestyle modifications, including smoking cessation, adopting a heart-healthy diet, and adhering strictly to prescribed antiplatelet and cholesterol-lowering therapies.
